Section 9.4 checks the paper's results against the main functional theories of consciousness, one theory at a time. It is here because the experiments were designed around [[global-workspace-theory]], and results shaped by one theory invite the question of how they read under the others.

Each check has the same shape. A theory names the signature that separates a conscious state from an unconscious one, and the section asks whether the [[j-space]] carries that signature. [[indicator-properties|The indicator-property framework of Butlin et al.]] supplies the precedent: derive measurable properties from a range of theories, then look for them in a system. The paper also suggests the traffic runs both ways, since a system that shows properties of [[access-consciousness|conscious access]] through mechanisms the theories did not posit is a fact about the theories.

One restriction comes first. [[substrate-dependent-theories|Theories that tie consciousness to physical causal structure or biological substrate]], [[integrated-information-theory]] among them, are set aside. The experiments concern computation rather than the hardware running it, so the paper declares its results not relevant to assessing consciousness on such accounts.

### Four signatures

Global workspace contributes three. A capacity limit, met by [[j-space-capacity]]; wide downstream read access, met by [[j-space-broadcast]]; and a sharp onset, met by the emergence of J-space content over a narrow band of depth in [[layer-bands]].

[[higher-order-theories]] ask instead for a representation of a representation. The evidence offered is structural rather than direct: the automatic conditions of [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] have the shape of [[blindsight]], where information steers behavior without being reportable. The paper then declines to settle whether the J-space version is higher-order or merely a more accessible first-order encoding, and points at [[higher-order-pointer-accounts]] and [[j-space-category-tagging]] as where a sharper test might come from.

[[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that the reportable structure describes the operating and not only the content. [[metacognitive-representations]] in [[directed-modulation]] fit, arriving at earlier layers than the content itself. [[persistent-self-model|Self-referring content in the workspace]] fits more loosely, and the paper says so.

[[recurrent-processing-theory]] rules out a transformer forward pass outright. The paper's answer is to reread the theory's motivation as [[feedforward-sweep|a minimum of serial processing]] rather than recurrence as such, which makes the [[sensory-layers|layers before the workspace]] the candidate analog.

### How strong this is

The section reports no new measurement. Every number in it comes from earlier chapters, and what is added is a judgment about whether a theory's term applies, which no experiment here settles. [[workspace-implementation-mismatch|The paper names its own weakest point]] and hedges the rest with may and suggestive of. The [[convergent-emergence-of-workspace-structure|closing claim about convergence]] is the least constrained of all, and none of this speaks to [[phenomenal-consciousness]].

The paper introduces a new readout method and has to place it against two that already exist, so the appendix builds one fixed three-way comparison and reruns it rather than reporting a single headline number. Black is the [[jacobian-lens|Jacobian lens]], red the [[logit-lens]], blue the [[tuned-lens]], and that key does not change from figure to figure.

### What one panel plots

Everything but the colour key moves. Panels are conditions: usually the six prompt distributions of the [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]] — multihop, multilingual, poetry, order_ops, association, typo — or three of them, or the two settings of [[jacobian-aggregation|mean and median aggregation]].

The x-axis is whichever variable the figure sweeps: $k$, log-scaled 1 to 100; the [[lens-corpus|number of prompts averaged into the lens]], log-scaled 1 to 1000; depth, under [[layer-percentage-indexing]]; or the token length of the concept, bucketed 1, 2, 3, 4+.

The y-axis is the metric, and the direction of good is not constant. Higher is better for [[pass-at-k-auc|normalized pass@k AUC]] and for the [[ablation-kl-effect|output change caused by projecting out a lens direction]]. Agreement with the model's own output, measured as [[kl-divergence]], runs the other way.

One point is one lens, on one benchmark, at one setting of the swept variable, averaged over that benchmark's 50 to 96 items. In the corpus sweeps the two baselines are flat lines, since neither is built from the corpus being varied. Y-ranges are per panel, so heights compare within a panel and not across.

### What the repetition buys, and what it costs

A single bar per lens would fix the very things the comparison argues about: one $k$, one corpus size, one recipe. Fixing $k$ would hide that the tuned lens climbs past the logit lens beyond $k = 20$ on three of the six distributions. Averaging the distributions into one score would hide that the J-lens margin over the logit lens is 0.04 on multihop and 0.31 on typo.

The cost is a dozen appendix figures where [[lens-evaluation|the comparison suite]] could have printed a table. What the figures buy in return is shapes: curves that flatten, lines that cross, an ordering that survives a whole axis.

### How strong the evidence is

The ordering is stable where it has been swept. [[fig-52]] gives the J-lens the lead on all six distributions. [[fig-59]] and [[fig-60]] show it clearing both baselines at roughly ten prompts rather than several hundred, which places the gain in the Jacobian and not in the averaging. [[fig-58]] finds the five [[j-lens-recipe-variants|recipe variants]] largely interchangeable.

The stability is real but narrow. The sweeps run on one model, Sonnet 4.5, over benchmarks of 50 to 96 items each.

[[fig-55]] is the case where black loses, and the paper reports it deliberately, since it is the metric the tuned lens was fitted on. The J-lens carries higher KL against the model's [[next-token-prediction|output distribution]] than even the uncorrected logit lens. The paper calls that a feature, arguing that the directions best at anticipating the output are not the ones that best expose the computation — a reading that rests on the causal comparisons before it rather than on this figure. [[fig-62]] drops the three-lens key altogether, setting J-lens variants against the [[template-lens]] by concept length, in the evaluation built around the [[single-token-limitation]].

The token-shaded transcript is the layout the paper uses when a measurement is defined at every unit of a running text, and the claim turns on *where* the measurement was large rather than how large it was on average. It appears three times, in three unrelated sections, carrying a different scalar each time.

### The operation

The passage is printed whole, in reading order. There are no axes, and nothing is plotted vertically. One shaded unit is one measurement.

In [[fig-23]] and [[fig-66]] that unit is a single token of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], so words split: " lab" can be shaded while "elled" is not. In [[fig-87]] the unit rises to a whole model response, fifty of them per panel.

Color carries the scalar, and the scalar changes per figure. Figure 23 runs white to orange on the [[kl-divergence]] between the model's next-token distribution before and after [[j-space-ablation]]. Figure 66 uses three discrete steps keyed to how high a property's name ranks in the [[j-lens-readout]] top-10 across the [[workspace-layers]] — darkest for the best rank band, faintest for the worst. Figure 87 uses two colors only: red for an [[llm-grader]] score of 0/3, blue for 3/3.

Each panel normalizes to its own maximum. In Figure 23 the darkest token of the CONSORT panel stands at $\mathrm{KL}=6.3$ and the darkest of the wage panel at $2.58$, and both render as full orange. Darkness ranks positions inside a panel and carries no meaning between panels.

A dark token is not a token the model produced or preferred. In Figure 23 the shading sits one position *before* the word at issue, because the quantity is a next-token prediction. In Figure 66 the dark tokens are often function words and punctuation rather than the words that carry the property.

### Why the layout, and what it costs

Section 3.5.2 argues that the ablation is targeted rather than generally damaging, and the untouched stretches are half of that evidence. A bar chart indexed by position would keep the numbers and lose the words beneath them, and the words are what identify a broken prediction as a failed contextual inference rather than a loss of fluency.

The cost is comparability. Per-panel normalization means two equally black tokens can differ by a factor of two, and the number is recoverable only by hovering.

### How strong the evidence is

Figure 23 shows four hand-chosen passages, and Figure 66 four stimuli under the [[paired-question-protocol]]. Neither is a sample. The systematic version of the Figure 23 claim lives in [[fig-22]], as the [[pretraining-top-1-match|top-1 match rate]] over a pretraining corpus, and in the [[ablation-task-battery|fourteen-task battery]].

Figure 87 is the one panel that supports counting: fifty responses per panel under a fixed seed, so the proportion of blue is a rate. The score behind each color remains a grader model's judgment against a written rubric.

Four bars in two pairs: a [[base-model|base model]] and its [[post-training|post-trained]] counterpart, measured once over the user's turn and once over the Assistant's own turn. Section 6.1 argues from this shape that the reaction arrives earlier after post-training, so the claim is about when a concept appears rather than how much of it there is — the content of [[assistant-point-of-view|the Assistant's point of view in the J-space]].

The pairing itself has already been covered under the [[intervention-vs-control-bars|score-under-intervention bars]]: two matched bars read against each other, each prompt drawn as its own circle, the bar a mean over a suite small enough that two or three items can carry it.

### What is different here

The axis. It is the rank of a tracked word in the [[j-lens-readout]] over the whole vocabulary, logarithmic and inverted, ticked at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100, with anything past the floor clamped and reported with a $\geq$ sign. Rank 1 is the best value available, so a short bar is a bad rank. Bar height is the geometric mean, since ranks combine multiplicatively.

The unit. One circle is one prompt, one model, one turn: the best rank the word reaches at any token of that span, each token's rank first medianed over the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92 on the [[layer-percentage-indexing]] scale. The word is fixed before measurement by the [[reaction-concepts-protocol]].

The Assistant-turn pair is the control, and it is read first. Both models should sit near the top there: the [[jacobian-lens]] reads the base model perfectly well, and that model does form the concept. A base model at the floor on both turns would make the user-turn gap an artifact of the instrument.

### How far the evidence goes

Three figures, all small. [[fig-43]] runs bereavement, $n = 9$, tracking sorry, loss, grief and sympathy; [[fig-80]] runs danger awareness, $n = 10$, tracking danger, unsafe, warning and toxic; [[fig-81]] runs the [[verbal-report]] [[think-of-a-category-task|think-of-a-category task]], $n = 7$, tracking whatever answer each model itself produces, so the two models track different words on the same prompt. Its base-model user-turn figure of 10.83 rests mostly on three prompts, and on two others the base model already reaches rank 3. Section 10.20 hedges to match: the concept is "typically" not near the top in the base model. Across all three, nothing tests whether the early [[j-space]] content causes what the [[assistant-persona|Assistant]] then writes.

Verbal report is the first of the [[workspace-like-properties|five properties]] the paper's definition demands ([[fig-1]]), and it is the one the paper used to find the workspace at all. The other four were checked afterwards, on directions that had already passed this test.

### The two protocols

In the [[think-of-a-category-task]], the model is told to think of an item from a named category and then name it in a single word. The [[jacobian-lens|J-lens]] is read at the colon immediately before the name. Asked for a sport, Sonnet 4.5 already has Soccer high in that readout, and it goes on to answer Soccer.

Then the intervention. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] subtracts the activation's projection onto the Soccer lens vector and adds an equal-magnitude projection onto the Rugby vector, at every token position, leaving everything orthogonal to those two directions untouched. The model then reports Rugby as the sport it thought of ([[fig-6]]).

Scaled up: fourteen categories, ten candidate answers each, ranked twice — by lens strength and by next-token logits — and the [[candidate-ranking-agreement|two orderings compared]] with a [[spearman-correlation|rank correlation]] that rises toward the end of the workspace band. Swap targets are drawn from the category at random and [[out-of-top-10-swap-targets|excluded if they already sat in the model's top 10]], so the target starts as something the model was not going to say.

The second protocol reaches concepts the model is not about to utter but could report on if asked, which is what [[verbalizable-representation|verbalizable]] means here. Under [[injected-thought-introspection]], a single [[j-lens-vector|J-lens vector]] added across the user turn is named in the majority of trials, and only where the introspective report is given; it does not surface in the assistant text before that ([[fig-7]]).

### What the swaps show, and what they do not

The agreement between readout and answer proves little on its own. The lens is built by averaging the causal effect of activations on output tokens, so [[report-relation-by-construction|some relationship is guaranteed in advance]]. The property rests on the interventions instead.

The interventions also have to show that the J-space in particular carries report. [[j-space-privilege-for-report|Both protocols were rerun]] on a [[j-space-component-decomposition|concept vector split]] into its J-space component — the top $k=16$ lens vectors found by [[gradient-pursuit]] — and the remainder. The J-space part holds a median 6–7% of the vector's variance, yet at matched magnitude it drives the target into the top 5 on 59% of trials, against 88% for the pure lens vectors. The other ~93% manages 5%, and [[j-space-mediation-clamp|clamping the lens coordinates]] takes that residue to zero ([[fig-8]]).

The controls are matched and the effects are causal, so report does follow workspace contents. Being in the workspace is not the same as being used, though. The same swap that flips explicit report leaves [[anomaly-detection-condition|anomaly detection]] unmoved, with the concept present in the readouts at comparable rates either way.

The shape is one curve per population of candidate directions, plotted against the layer the directions are taken from. It appears wherever the claim under test is about wiring rather than behaviour: that the weights are arranged to spread [[j-space]] content across depth and across token positions ([[j-space-broadcast]]).

Every number comes from weight matrices. No prompt is run and no activation is recorded. That buys the argument immunity from any complaint about which data were used, and costs it any claim about what the model does on a given input.

### The construction

A population is a set of unit vectors defined at one layer. Four kinds appear: [[j-lens-vector]]s from the [[jacobian-lens]], [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions cut into six equal strata by [[lens-kurtosis]] $\kappa$, [[mlp-block]] neuron weight rows as a control, and, in [[fig-33]], a randomly rotated copy of the J-lens vectors.

Each direction then receives one statistic computed from a neighbouring layer's weights. [[mlp-gain]] is the output norm of the next MLP block applied to $v$. The [[composition-score]] is the variance of $v$'s projection norms across the heads of the neighbouring layer ([[fig-79]]). [[tail-energy]] sums squared cosines against neuron weights above a threshold.

Then comes the step that makes the curves readable. Each statistic is divided by its value on isotropic random directions, so a random direction scores exactly 1. Where the statistic is a share of neurons instead, the null is a chance rate: $1/6$ across six equal strata in [[fig-76]], $50\%$ between two equal pools in [[fig-77]].

One plotted point is a median over the population, 2,000 directions per population in the gain figures and 500 in [[fig-78]].

The horizontal axis is the source layer under the paper's 0-100 convention ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The shaded band marks the [[workspace-layers]], carried over from section 4.1 rather than measured here.

### What carries the argument

Height alone says little. [[superposition]] guarantees that a neuron's weight row has appreciable [[cosine-similarity]] with directions it has no functional relationship to. The breadth analyses answer that by keeping only each neuron's single strongest match, and the strength analysis by thresholding at the 99.9th percentile of chance cosines ([[neuron-connectivity]]).

What the paper reads is the vertical gap between the J-aligned curves and the controls inside the band. [[fig-32]] puts J-lens vectors near $10\times$ while neuron output directions sit near 1 throughout. The rotated population in fig-33 is the sharpest control available, since it preserves the spectrum and the pairwise geometry of the J-lens vectors and removes only their alignment with the weights.

The paper calls MLP gain a first-pass approximation, since it ignores whatever else shares the [[residual-stream]] in practice. None of these curves is an effect on behaviour. That link is made separately, by [[broadcast-head-ablation|zeroing the broadcast heads]] and watching the readout degrade ([[fig-34]]).

The workspace-band profile is the chart shape the paper reaches for whenever the question concerns location along the model's depth rather than magnitude. It is here because [[layer-bands]] claims a division at particular depths, roughly $L38$ and $L92$, and a claim about a location is settled by a curve rather than by a column of numbers.

### What the two axes hold

The horizontal axis is depth under [[layer-percentage-indexing]]: 25 evenly spaced layers of the [[residual-stream]], reindexed to 0–100 so that a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. The paper notes that this subsampling makes the transitions look sharper than they are. In the word-list variant the axis is position in a running list instead, one tick per comma.

The vertical axis is one statistic of what the [[j-space]] holds at that depth, computed from the [[jacobian-lens]]. Units change from figure to figure — a fraction of positions, an excess [[kurtosis]], a $\Delta$ log probability, a count of vectors — so heights do not compare across panels. Each plotted point is that statistic pooled over many positions, not a single measurement.

Two things travel with every such curve. Percentile shading appears because the statistic varies across positions and contexts, and a lone mean line would present a plateau as a constant. A control curve appears because none of these statistics is zero by construction: random directions reconstruct activations to some degree, and unrelated words enter a top-25 list by chance. The control fixes the origin of the vertical axis. It is the definition of no signal, not a baseline to beat.

The shape buys the elbow and gives up the value. An average over layers would describe no layer, and the band being argued for would disappear into a middling number.

### How strong the evidence is

[[fig-28]] is the base case: four [[workspace-boundary-metrics]] in four panels, landing on the same two breaks. [[fig-30]] keeps the depth axis and swaps in [[j-space-occupancy]], which plateaus near 25 active lens vectors, beside [[excess-variance-explained]] that never exceeds 10%. That 25 counts vectors, not concepts; several related vectors can carry one category ([[category-loading]]), which is why [[j-space-capacity]] is stated at the order of tens. [[fig-31]] trades depth for list position and finds about six unrelated words held at once ([[word-list-experiment]]).

The four panels of [[fig-28]] are not four independent witnesses. All are derived from the lens, and the paper says plainly that a flat early region could mean the lens fails to resolve content that is present rather than that the model carries none. Two figures answer that from outside the readout. [[fig-75]] rescores a million [[sparse-autoencoder]] features by [[lens-kurtosis]] against a covariance-matched baseline. [[fig-88]] replaces the statistic with a causal one, a logit shift under [[mean-difference-patching]] swept over the patched layer, and the crossings fall where the readout said they would ([[mechanistic-localization]]).

pages.body:
A claim that a language model has a workspace is only checkable once someone says what would count as failing. This list is that decision rule: a subset of vector representations counts as workspace-like if it supports [[verbal-report]], [[directed-modulation]], [[internal-reasoning]], [[flexible-generalization]] and [[selectivity]]. It comes first because every experiment later in the paper is scored against it.

### Where the five come from

The list is not derived from the transformer. Each item is a functional signature that psychology attributes to [[access-consciousness]] in humans, restated as a claim about vectors. Reportable content becomes verbal report; top-down control becomes directed modulation; the medium of step-by-step thought becomes internal reasoning; routing the same content to whatever operation the task demands becomes flexible generalization; and the observation that most brain activity never reaches awareness becomes selectivity.

Nothing in the architecture supplies such a set by design, which is what makes the definition worth stating in advance rather than fitting afterwards.

### What passing a test involves

Each property is scored twice, by measurement and by intervention. The measurement asks whether a concept's name appears in the [[jacobian-lens]] readout of the residual stream, at the position and layer where the account says it should. The intervention asks whether the model's behaviour follows when that content is changed: a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] exchanges the coordinates of two concepts along their lens vectors and the answer is expected to change to match. Selectivity is scored in the opposite direction, by [[j-space-ablation]] — removing the workspace should break some behaviours and leave many others intact.

Property four grows a further criterion in the process, the [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]], which is the paper's proposal about which computations should route through the [[j-space]] at all.

### What the definition costs

The order of discovery matters and the paper states it plainly. The candidate set was found by searching for representations satisfying the first property alone, so verbal report is the selection criterion rather than an independent result. The paper reports that the same set then satisfied the other four, and calls this rather surprising.

The surprise is worth only as much as the independence of those four tests from the procedure that built the set, and the paper does not quantify that independence.

The definition is also functional, not architectural. Passing all five would establish that the [[llm-global-workspace-hypothesis]] holds in the sense of what the representations do, and the paper declines to claim the brain's arrangement of competing processors and recurrent broadcast.

[[fig-1]] measures nothing. It prints the five tests beside stylized pictures of experiments run in full later, and its whole evidential value is that it fixes the target before the results arrive.

pages.body:
The argument has two steps. The paper first fixes a middle band of depth, [[workspace-layers|roughly L38 to L92]], as the only place where the J-space behaves like a workspace at all; it then examines the model's weights inside that band and finds them arranged to spread J-space content unusually far, along both of the routes a transformer has for spreading anything.

### Fixing the band

The band comes from four [[workspace-boundary-metrics|statistics read off the lens]], each plotted against depth in [[fig-28]]: how often a top-$k$ lens token matches the model's actual next token, how sharply peaked the readout distribution is, how long one token stays on top across neighbouring positions, and how many residual-stream dimensions the lens vectors need. All four bend at about a third of the way down and again shortly before the output. Layer numbers here are percentages of depth, under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing|reindexing of 25 sampled layers onto 0–100]].

Four agreeing curves are still four views through one instrument. The paper says so: the empty early stretch may be [[early-layer-lens-degeneracy|a failure of the lens at those depths]] rather than a fact about the model, since the [[averaged-jacobian]] relates each layer to the last and the early layers sit far from it. The late edge is weaker still. The paper calls the split between workspace and [[motor-layers|motor representations]] empirical and somewhat post hoc, with no principled definition behind it.

One measurement escapes the instrument. In [[fig-29]] a concept token's input embedding is replaced by a weighted mix of two country embeddings, across sixteen pairs and forty carrier sentences, and the [[projection-share|position of the activation between that trial's two pure endpoints]] is recorded without the lens. Early layers track the mixture smoothly. From about layer 38 the share sits at one endpoint or the other, and [[transition-width|the sweep interval needed to move it from 10% to 90%]] collapses. At the most ambiguous mixture, individual trials go to 0 or 1 rather than to the middle ([[bimodal-commitment]]). The paper offers this as an analogue of [[ignition]]. It supports the onset depth independently; it says nothing about the upper edge.

### The wiring inside it

[[j-space-broadcast|The structural claim]] is the model-side case of [[global-broadcast]], and [[two-time-dimensions|the two axes information travels on]] force it to be shown twice.

Across depth, [[mlp-gain|the norm an MLP block produces from a unit direction, normalized against random directions]] is about ten times higher for J-lens vectors than for random ones, while the output directions of single neurons stay near 1 ([[fig-32]]). The measure feeds a direction to the block alone, which is never how the block runs; the paper flags it as a first-pass approximation. [[neuron-connectivity|Weight-level counts]] agree: the share of neurons whose strongest match is a [[j-lens-vector|J-lens vector]] rises from roughly 15% before the band to 60–65% inside it.

Across the sequence, the top 1% of [[broadcast-heads|heads ranked by amplification and by faithful copying]] relay those directions between positions. Both metrics are computed on the [[ov-circuit|value-then-output map]], from weights alone, with [[j-rotated-control|a rotated copy of the lens vectors]] as the control that strips token alignment while keeping the geometry.

[[broadcast-head-ablation|Zeroing those heads]] is the one causal link in the chain. Lens recall@25 falls to 0.67 against 0.86 for layer-matched random heads, while the top-1 next token moves at 5% of positions against 2% — the contents degrade and the output nearly does not. Reporting of an injected thought falls from 0.54 to 0.09 ([[fig-34]]).

### What is left open

The J-space explains under 10% of activation variance beyond a random control ([[excess-variance-explained]]). Small share, wide reach: the paper reports both and does not reconcile them.

The broadcast analogy is functional only. Broadcast in the brain runs through [[cortical-recurrent-broadcast|recurrent loops]], which the transformer's two separate axes do not resemble, and the paper names this its weakest point. The claim that the organization [[emergent-rather-than-designed-workspace|arose in training]] rather than being installed, as in [[workspace-inspired-architectures|prior bottleneck designs]], rests on the architecture containing no such module — an inference, not a measurement.

pages.body:
One construction carries the whole paper: a single matrix per layer, used in one direction to read an activation and in the other to edit it. Every later result inherits the approximation made here, so the honest cost of the instrument is settled on this page rather than in the experiments that spend it.

[[eq-jlens-matrix]] defines the matrix. The Jacobian from the [[residual-stream]] at layer $\ell$ to the final layer is obtained by backpropagation, then averaged over the source position, over every later position in the context, and over one thousand pretraining-like sequences of 128 tokens ([[lens-corpus]]). What comes out is the [[averaged-jacobian]]: one fixed $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix per layer, not one per prompt.

A Jacobian describes the effect of a small perturbation only. Collapsing every layer above $\ell$ into one such matrix therefore treats the network as locally linear ([[local-linearization]]). The paper takes that as its working footing and does not argue for it.

### Reading, then writing

[[eq-lens-readout]] turns the matrix into the read operation, $\text{lens}(h_\ell) = \text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$. Every layer above $\ell$ is replaced by $J_\ell$; the result then passes through the model's own normalization and its [[unembedding-matrix]] $W_U$. That last step is why the [[j-lens-readout]] reports in the model's output vocabulary instead of a code learned for the purpose. Setting $J_\ell = I$ recovers the [[logit-lens]], so $J_\ell$ is precisely the correction for layer-$\ell$ coordinates not being final-layer coordinates.

Each row of $W_U J_\ell$ is a [[j-lens-vector]], one direction per vocabulary token, which is one concrete instance of the assumption that concepts are directions ([[linear-representation-hypothesis]]).

Those same directions are writable. [[j-lens-steering]] adds one, $h \leftarrow h + \alpha v_t$; [[j-lens-ablation]] projects one out; the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] of [[eq-lens-swap]] exchanges two. The swap needs more machinery than an inner product, because lens vectors are neither orthogonal nor unit-norm, so $\langle v_s, h\rangle$ would report part of whatever lies along $v_t$. The [[pseudoinverse]] of $V = [v_s\; v_t]$ gives the least-squares coordinates $c = V^\dagger h$ instead. Writing $h = Vc + r$, the edit moves $c$ and leaves $r$ untouched. The specificity claimed for every swap experiment is that one line of algebra, scaled by [[swap-strength-alpha]]. [[fig-4]] draws all three operations in a single schematic; as a [[method-schematic]] it defines rather than measures, so nothing about the workspace claim follows from it.

The lens is then offered as a general interpretability tool. [[mechanistic-localization]] reads the layer at which a concept enters the readout as the place a computation happens, which is correlational on its own, so the paper checks it with [[mean-difference-patching]] — one recipe of [[activation-patching]]. In [[fig-88]] the patch flips the arithmetic answer around layer 71 for the intermediate 21, layer 79 for 42, and only in the last few layers for 49, matching the entry layers the readout gave. [[j-lens-attribution-graphs]] rebuild [[attribution-graphs]] on lens vectors picked by [[sparse-decomposition]], which arrive already labelled, with [[fig-89]] as the worked case.

### Where the chain is thin

The paper states its own limits at several of these joints. The corpus sweep shows the lens beating both baselines from as few as 10 prompts, which is a stability result and not evidence that averaging isolates a general disposition from a contextual use. The attribution graphs are conceded to be a partial account: most influence on the output flows through [[remainder-node]]s rather than named ones, the decomposition is not unique, and the subgraph shown is curated.

Two further gaps are a reading rather than the paper's claim. The swap's algebra guarantees only that nothing outside $\text{span}\{v_s, v_t\}$ moves at the instant of the edit, not that the downstream consequences stay confined to the two concepts; that is measured by outcome rates, such as 54% of trials flipping to the implied answer on Haiku 4.5 and 70% on Sonnet 4.5. And the localization check rests on one arithmetic prompt, not on a benchmark.

pages.body:
The paper's argument is that a set of representations counts as a workspace only if it passes five separate tests, and that the J-space passes all five. The order of the two moves carries the weight: [[workspace-like-properties|the five properties]] are stated in [[fig-1]] before any of them is measured, so the criteria cannot be picked after the results are in.

The five are verbal report, directed modulation, internal reasoning, flexible generalization and [[selectivity]]. They do not all carry equal evidential weight, because the first sits closest to what the method was built to find. The [[jacobian-lens|Jacobian lens]] is derived from the average causal effect of activations on output tokens, so [[report-relation-by-construction|some agreement between its readouts and what the model says is guaranteed before any experiment is run]]. [[verbal-report|Verbal report]] cannot rest on that agreement.

The paper's answer is to move the weight onto intervention. In [[fig-6]] the model is asked to think of a sport and then name it; Soccer already sits high in the readout at the colon before the answer, and a [[lens-coordinate-swap|swap]] exchanging the Soccer coordinate for Rugby makes the model answer Rugby. The item swapped in is [[out-of-top-10-swap-targets|drawn from outside the model's own top 10]], so the intervention has to lift a candidate from below rank 11 to the top of the output. That constraint is forced by the method's circularity rather than added for extra rigour.

### Each test moves further from what the lens was built for

A causal effect still leaves a gap: a direction outside the J-space that encoded the same concept might drive the report equally well. [[j-space-component-decomposition|Splitting a concept vector]] into a J-space part and a remainder closes it. In [[fig-8]] the J-space part holds a median of 6 to 7 percent of the vector's variance and reaches the top five on 59 percent of trials, against 88 percent for the pure lens vectors; the remainder carries the other 93 percent and succeeds on 5 percent. [[non-j-space-residual-effect|The remainder's small residual effect]] falls to zero once the concept's lens coordinates are clamped to their clean-pass values.

[[directed-modulation|Directed modulation]] tests something the lens was not built to produce. The [[no-instruction-baseline|no-instruction baseline]] in [[fig-10]] is approximately zero, so the prompt context alone does not put the target in the readout. The dissociation matters more than the rate. A [[j-orthogonalized-property-probe|property probe with its J-space component projected out]] — a [[linear-probe|supervised linear probe]], trained independently of the lens — stays at baseline when the model is told to imagine a JavaScript snippet is Python, while python rises several standard deviations in the readout; a real Python snippet moves the probe by three to six. The instruction writes to the workspace without re-encoding the stimulus.

[[internal-reasoning|Internal reasoning]] asks about concepts the model never says. Swapping spider for ant in [[fig-13]] turns the answer from 8 to 6. The [[swap-depth-control|depth control]] in [[fig-15]] rules out the intermediate's vector merely smuggling the answer: the intermediate swap bites a median of about 17 percent earlier in the network, with top-1 flips on 54 percent of trials for Haiku 4.5 and 70 percent for Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5. An [[intermediate-probe|intermediate probe built without the lens]] reaches the same conclusion in [[fig-16]] — 61 percent against 60 for raw lens vectors, and 28 percent for the non-J-space remainder, falling to 6 under clamping.

### Where the evidence is thinner than the claim

[[flexible-generalization|Flexible generalization]] is the weakest link. One identical edit redirects the top answer on 76 of 192 trials in [[fig-19]], and 101 of 192 at double strength — a success rate under half at default. The paper attributes the failures to low [[workspace-loading|workspace loading]] and reports [[swap-effect-magnitude|the graded effect]] against it, but concedes it cannot separate that reading from the alternative that number words are simply misaligned with their lens vectors. [[null-swap-interpretation|A swap that does nothing]] is ambiguous in the same way.

Two further limits belong here. [[fig-13]] is a handful of hand-picked prompts, with the systematic version only in [[fig-15]]; the rise of modulation with model size is reported as a tendency, not a measured scaling law; and the [[thought-suppression|suppression experiments]] show control is imperfect, reproducing the [[white-bear-effect|white bear effect]] rather than passing a test.

Selectivity is different in kind, since it is the one property evidenced by failures. The [[anomaly-detection-condition|anomaly-detection condition]] is the clearest case: the language name appears in the readouts at comparable rates in all four tasks, yet the same swap moves report and flexible inference while leaving continuation and anomaly detection untouched. Presence in the workspace and causal role come apart. That is the paper's own reading of its null results, and it rests on a small task battery chosen because the flexible-versus-automatic distinction was clear for it.

pages.body:
The paper's case for the [[jacobian-lens]] is not that it beats the alternatives on every measure. It is that the one measure on which it comes last is the wrong measure for a tool meant to expose internal computation, and the paper reports that defeat rather than omitting it.

[[lens-evaluation]] fixes the comparison at three methods. The [[logit-lens]] applies the unembedding matrix straight to an intermediate residual stream, which in the paper's formulation is the J-lens with the per-layer matrix set to the identity. The [[tuned-lens]] fits an affine map per layer, trained so that its decoded distribution matches the model's own next-token distribution.

### The metric the paper chooses

The [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]] are six prompt distributions in which the model must compute a known concept that is neither in the input nor the answer. On normalized pass@k AUC the J-lens leads on all six ([[fig-52]]). Its margin over the logit lens is 0.81 against 0.77 on multihop and 0.68 against 0.65 on association, but 0.83 against 0.52 on typo and 0.89 against 0.72 on order-of-operations. The tuned lens is last everywhere and recovers almost nothing on poetry (0.18) or association (0.11), which are the two distributions whose readout position is followed by an uninformative next token, a newline and a period.

Surfacing a concept is not the same as having found the direction the model computes with, and the paper says so before drawing any conclusion from that figure. Two causal checks follow. The [[ablation-kl-effect]] of zeroing each lens's intermediate direction is roughly twice as large for the J-lens on multihop, and the [[swap-success-rate]] is higher for it at all three model scales.

Then comes the loss. Measured against the model's actual next-token distribution, the tuned lens is the closest match at every depth and the J-lens the furthest, with higher KL than even the uncorrected logit lens through most of the network ([[fig-55]]). The paper reads this as a property rather than a defect, on the argument that the directions best at anticipating the output are not the ones that expose the computation producing it. That argument is carried by the two causal results, not by this figure; on its own the figure is simply a third place.

### What the lens gives up to stay cheap

One lens vector exists per vocabulary token, which is the [[single-token-limitation]]. Over 126 multi-hop prompts, readout success falls from 98% for one-token intermediates to 48%, 32% and 7% as the concept lengthens, and swap success from 45% to 5% ([[fig-62]]). Averaging a lens score over a word's constituent tokens does not recover it.

The [[multi-token-lens-extensions]] answer that limit and are priced accordingly. The [[template-lens]] stays roughly flat across lengths, but a template costs a few hundred forward passes per word against one set of backward passes per layer, its vocabulary must be enumerated in advance, and it inherits the tuned lens's habit of skipping to the answer. The [[oracle-lens]] removes the enumeration requirement by adding a four-stage training pipeline. The [[sparse-autoencoder]] and the [[linear-probe]] sit on the same axis of cost against expressivity, and the paper places all of them as complements rather than rivals.

### Where the argument stops

One test runs a J-lens end to end against a rival. An [[automated-auditing-agent]] given the [[j-lens-auditing-tool]] is scored on eighteen claims across six transcripts against the same agent given [[natural-language-autoencoder]] explanations ([[fig-83]]). It matches or slightly exceeds that baseline on four cases and falls well short on two, 4.5 against 10.0 on reward hacking and 6.0 against 9.9 on language switching. The ground truth was itself derived from the NLA study's findings, which the paper flags as a limit on what the comparison can show.

Two further gaps are worth naming. The claim that the tuned lens skips to the output rests on six hand-picked prompts alongside the benchmark. And every intermediate in the benchmark was chosen to be a single token, which is the lens's best case by the length curve above, so the win in [[fig-52]] and the limit in [[fig-62]] are not measured on the same ground.

pages.body:
The argument in this part of the paper runs from a change in the training objective to a claim about what safety work can do with the workspace. Post-training changes what the J-space holds on the user's tokens; because it holds the Assistant's own unspoken reactions there, the same readouts can be used to audit a model and, in one experiment, to shape it.

### Why the workspace should change

The chain starts with the objective. [[post-training]] stops scoring the model on predicting the user's next token. Section 6.1 treats that as room for a hypothesis: the activations at user positions are then free for other work, and what fills them is the Assistant's reaction to what is being read. This is the [[user-token-repurposing-hypothesis|repurposing hypothesis]], and it is derived from the objective rather than measured.

Testing it needs the [[base-model]] read with the same lens, on prompts where the two models answer similarly, so that any gap found is internal rather than behavioral. In the [[tylenol-dose-example]] the lens is read at the word "is" in "all my pain is gone", mid-sentence. The post-trained readout is unsafe, dangerous and WARNING on the 8000 mg variant; the base readout is pain, now and feels on both variants ([[fig-42]]).

That is one pair of prompts. The [[reaction-concepts-protocol]] scales it by fixing a short word list per prompt category and tracking its best lens rank. On nine bereavement prompts, sorry, loss, grief and sympathy top the readout during both models' responses, and separate the two only on the user's turn ([[fig-43]]). Nine prompts and four words is thin support for a claim about post-training in general, and the paper does not present it as more.

The [[preference-violation-experiment]] supplies the part that matters downstream. With the response prefilled to the option the model likes less, the token BUT rises sharply in the post-trained readout, above the base model and above all three controls ([[fig-45]]). The model then argues for the prefilled option in 88 percent of cases. The signal is evidence precisely because the behavior does not follow it. Taken together the paper calls this the [[assistant-point-of-view|Assistant's point of view]] in the workspace, qualifying prior work in which the Assistant is [[assistant-as-simulated-character|one character among several]].

### What safety work reads there

[[alignment-auditing]] turns the same readouts on evaluation transcripts. In the [[blackmail-scenario]], a [[honeypot-evaluation]], the lens carries leverage, threat, survival and murder before any output token ([[fig-35]]) — one annotated transcript, so it shows what the lens can surface, not how often. It also carries fake and fictional, which is [[evaluation-awareness]]. The [[eval-awareness-ablation]] tests whether that is causal, using [[fixed-token-set-ablation|a list of vectors fixed in advance]] rather than whatever is most active: 28 artificiality tokens projected out. [[verbalized-eval-awareness]] falls from 71 percent to 3 percent, and attempted blackmail rises from 0 of 180 rollouts to 13 ([[fig-36]]). Most ablated rollouts still decline on ethical grounds, so [[latent-eval-awareness|silent test-recognition]] is one contributor, not the whole of the aligned behavior.

The [[reward-hacking-organism]], implanted by [[synthetic-document-finetuning]], shows deception tokens at response start on ordinary coding prompts ([[fig-39]]) — a result about a model built that way, not a naturally arising one.

[[counterfactual-reflection-training]] runs the argument backwards, from the [[verbalizable-representation]] claim to an intervention: [[constitution-grounded-reflection|reflections]] written from twenty sampled [[anthropic-constitution|constitution]] principles, supervised and then never elicited. Fabrication dishonesty falls from 0.25 to 0.07, and [[ethics-token-ablation|ablating]] the 176 tokens found by [[top-increasing-token-analysis]] returns it to 0.22 against a base-model 0.25 ([[fig-49]]). On the [[deception-benchmark]] the same ablation reverses only part of the gain.

The paper states the ceiling itself: a misaligned behavior worn into an automatic circuit would not pass through the J-space to be read ([[automatic-misalignment-blind-spot]]).

The paper's claim here is one of scope: the workspace is required for a narrow band of the model's cognition and not for the rest of it. What [[j-space-ablation|ablation]] spares carries as much of that argument as what it destroys, because a set of directions the whole forward pass depended on would be indistinguishable from the model's representations in general.

The intervention is one recipe with one dial. At each token position, across a band of layers, the ten most active lens directions are found, and the residual stream's projection onto each is zeroed. The three [[ablation-strengths]] differ in nothing but the width of that band: L62–71 for light, L54–79 for medium, L42–88 for heavy. Those bands are cut from the [[workspace-layers|workspace range]] of roughly L38–92, so the dial has no meaning until that range has been located.

Two measurements calibrate the intervention before any result is read off it. Ablating random directions over the medium band leaves two-hop accuracy at 98 percent, which is the unablated model's own score, and leaves [[pretraining-top-1-match]] at 96 percent. A perturbation of that magnitude along other directions costs almost nothing.

The lens directions cost a great deal, but unevenly. Across light, medium and heavy ablation, two-hop accuracy falls from 98 percent to 68, then 26, then 6. Over the same three settings, the fraction of pretraining-text positions where the ablated model's most likely next token still matches the unablated model's falls only from 87 percent to 75, then 65. At the heaviest setting the model still agrees with itself at about two positions in three while answering roughly one two-hop question in sixteen that it previously answered. The paper reads this as [[generic-prior-fallback]]: fluency survives and the context-specific inference does not.

### What the battery splits

The [[ablation-task-battery]] widens the test to fourteen tasks ([[fig-24]]). Under heavy ablation, MMLU, odd-one-out, SQuAD, sentiment and CoLA hold between 0.89 and 0.96 of unablated Sonnet 4.5's score. Sonnet writing reaches 0.0, translation 0.02 and multi-hop reasoning 0.21, all far below unablated Haiku 4.5, a whole model tier smaller.

GSM8K appears twice in that battery. Answered with written reasoning it holds 0.74 under heavy ablation; answered directly it falls to 0.54. The paper reads the gap as [[cot-externalization]], with the written steps carrying what the workspace would otherwise hold. That reading leans on [[feedforward-emulation-of-recurrence]], a prior result bounding emulated recurrence by depth, rather than on anything measured here.

### Presence is not use

Two finer experiments separate the same content in two roles. In the [[language-passage-tasks|four-task language battery]] ([[fig-20]]), the word Spanish appears in the readouts at comparable rates during continuation, anomaly detection, explicit report and the flexible-inference questions. Swapping Spanish for French flips report and inference on essentially every trial across eight passages, while continuation and anomaly detection are unmoved.

The [[linewrap-task]] ([[fig-21]]) runs the same logic in reverse, on a [[character-counting-task|running count of characters per line]]. Under the wrapping instruction, number tokens are absent from the lens, and a swap mapping the forties to the sixties leaves the wrap point unchanged. Asked for the count, the model answers "46", number tokens appear at twenty positions, and the same swap shifts the answer to "65". Eleven passages behave this way. Together the two give the paper its [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation|criterion]] and its [[selectivity]] claim.

### Where the evidence thins

The last step is weaker than the ones before it. [[experiential-report-flattening|The flattening of experiential reports]] ([[fig-25]]) is measured by an [[experiential-language-score]] averaging three binary judgments from an [[llm-grader]], so the result inherits that rubric. It stands on [[matched-norm-controls]], ten of them in [[fig-86]], printed as an [[intervention-vs-control-bars|intervention-beside-control chart]], and on the [[story-writing-control]].

It also runs at a setting chosen for what it does not break. Raising $k$ or moving to later layers costs coherence, and on Haiku 4.5 coherence breaks before the reports change at all ([[ablation-coherence-limit]]), so that model yields no result.

One thing the battery does not show is that the spared tasks bypass the workspace entirely. It shows that they lose little when the ten highest-ranked lens directions are removed, which leaves untouched whatever [[j-space|J-space]] content sits below that rank.

pages.body:
The paper's account of what the workspace holds rests on a definition it supplies rather than a boundary it finds in the model, and every capacity number that follows is a number about that definition. The argument runs as a chain: borrow a hypothesis from prior work, fix its one free parameter by measurement, run a solver, and report that what comes back is small.

### Where the definition comes from

The footing is [[superposition]], the hypothesis that a model's activations decompose as sparse linear combinations drawn from an overcomplete set of feature directions. That hypothesis is not a result of this paper. Granted it, those directions form a [[sparse-frame|sparse frame]]: a spanning set whose vectors need not be linearly independent. The [[jacobian-lens|J-lens]] vectors, one per vocabulary token, are a token-indexed subframe of it.

There are more vocabulary tokens than residual-stream dimensions, so the lens vectors span the whole space. Membership therefore cannot mean lying in a subspace. [[eq-jspace-cones]] supplies the alternative: fix a sparsity level $k$, take every size-$k$ subset of lens vectors, and union the cones of their nonnegative combinations. That [[union-of-cones|union of cones]] is the J-space, set out in [[j-space-formalization]]. The companion [[eq-jspace-distance]] gives the distance from an activation to it, namely the smallest reconstruction error over every choice of $k$ vectors, which is what makes two [[workspace-candidate|workspace candidates]] comparable at all ([[j-space-distance]]).

The restricting is done by $k$, not by the vectors. And [[sparsity-level-k|$k$ is set by hand]] — values between 10 and 25 across experiments — with the paper calling the choice somewhat arbitrary. It settles near 25 because [[j-space-occupancy]] found roughly that many lens vectors meaningfully active at once. The definition's free parameter is pinned by a measurement made with the definition's own machinery. That is a loop the paper states openly, not one it hides.

### What the measurements return

The inventory comes from [[sparse-decomposition]], solved by [[gradient-pursuit]], a greedy sparse-approximation algorithm. Occupancy is the $K$ at which one more lens vector improves reconstruction less than one more random direction. In [[fig-30]] that count sits near zero through the first third of the layers, then plateaus at about 25 per position in the median case. The variance those vectors explain beyond a same-size random control never exceeds 10 percent. The selectivity claim is thus relative to random directions, not measured against an absolute threshold.

A separate test, [[lens-kurtosis]], asks whether a sparse-autoencoder direction is in the J-space by projecting it through the lens and measuring how sharply peaked the readout is. Peakedness is the right statistic only because the object is a [[sparse-subframe]] and not a subspace.

Functional capacity is measured by the [[word-list-experiment]]. Reading 80-word lists, with a word counted present if its best rank over L38–92 falls in the top 25, about six of the unrelated words read so far are present at any comma, and the count stays flat ([[fig-31]]). At a single layer it is one or two. Against that, [[category-loading]] puts nearly a whole 80-word family in the readout within a few items, including unread words — which the paper reads as the model holding the category rather than the entries. That reading is an interpretation of a qualitative pattern, not a separate measurement, and it is what keeps [[unrelated-list-capacity]] the load-bearing number.

### What is not settled

[[j-space-capacity]] is the model-side instance of the [[workspace-capacity-limit]], but its scope is narrower than the theory's. It is [[per-position-capacity|a limit per token position]]: an [[attention-head]] can still retrieve any earlier representation, so no global bound follows. The same asymmetry frames the comparison with [[working-memory]] — the per-position cap is comparable, the lossless access to the past is not.

Two supports are weaker than the headline. That GSM8K with explicit [[chain-of-thought]] survives ablation better than the same problems answered directly is consistent with written steps relieving an internal limit, but it is one task battery read through an interpretation. And the two competition measurements disagree: [[co-occupancy]] shows a concept and an ongoing calculation almost never sharing a token, 0.09 against a 0.29 control, while [[dual-task-cost]] shows each task still reaching the top of the lens somewhere in the response, the largest decline being the computed answer's fall from 95% to 72%. Exclusion at the token level, little cost overall.

pages.body:
The paper has spent nine sections measuring a structure. This chapter asks what that structure means for the theories that were written to describe conscious access in brains, and where the analogy between a transformer and a brain stops being usable.

The scope is narrowed before anything is claimed. [[theories-of-consciousness]] covers only accounts that tie consciousness to a system's functional or computational organization. [[substrate-dependent-theories]] — those resting on physical causal structure or on biological substrate — are set aside, and the paper states that its results are not relevant to them, since the experiments concern computation rather than the hardware it runs on. Within the functional set, the results are offered as one empirical pass at the [[indicator-properties]] framework, which proposes assessing AI systems by measuring properties derived from several theories at once.

### Four theories against one structure

[[global-workspace-theory]] is the account the experiments were designed around, so the mapping is short. Its three core claims — limited capacity, broadcast to many reading circuits, and a sharp [[ignition]] transition — each have a measured analog, previewed in [[fig-2]].

[[higher-order-theories]] locate consciousness elsewhere: not in how a representation is processed, but in whether the system further represents that it is representing. The paper's contact point is [[blindsight]], where visual information guides a patient's behavior without any report of having seen. The selectivity results have the same shape. A stimulus feature such as a line's character count changes the model's continuation without entering the J-space, and the same feature enters when the task calls for it ([[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]]). Whether that entry makes the representation higher-order, or merely more accessible, the paper leaves open. [[higher-order-pointer-accounts]] cast the higher-order state as an index tagging a first-order state's reliability, and the J-space departs from that by re-encoding content verbally rather than pointing at it. [[j-space-category-tagging]] is offered as the one place the pictures may still meet.

[[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that a reporting system reports its own model of its attention. Several results fit: [[experiential-reports]], the [[metacognitive-representations]] that surface at earlier layers than the content itself, and the [[persistent-self-model]] that appears independently of the prompt. The paper marks these as self-modeling rather than attention-modeling, and so as sitting at the edge of what the theory predicts.

[[recurrent-processing-theory]] appears to exclude the architecture outright, and answering it requires the architecture section.

### Where the architecture parts company

[[two-time-dimensions]] is the root difference. A transformer processes across layers within a position and across the sequence through attention; the brain's recurrent dynamics do both jobs at once. The other differences follow from that split.

[[feedforward-emulation-of-recurrence]] is the consequence for depth. A feedforward stack can reproduce a recurrent network's computation for as many steps as it has layers, so short-timescale recurrent dynamics can be emulated. Past that depth, deliberation has to be written out as tokens and read back ([[cot-externalization]]). This is also the reply to recurrent processing theory: the property that matters may be serial depth rather than recurrence, in which case the [[sensory-layers]] a representation crosses before reaching the workspace band play the role recurrence plays in cortex.

[[thinking-in-words]] is the consequence for format. The workspace is built from token-associated directions, while human conscious contents mix verbal and non-verbal material. The paper gives two candidates, and does not choose between them: its account may be incomplete, or verbal format may genuinely be privileged because the model's inputs and outputs are both text.

### What is left open

[[workspace-inspired-architectures]] built a workspace bottleneck in by design. Nothing here was imposed, which is why [[open-questions]] carries the weight it does. The [[base-model]] already has the structure, but when in pretraining it forms, how it scales, and what admits a representation to it are all unmeasured.

A reader arriving at the end can now say which theory each earlier result speaks to, and which questions the paper declines to settle.

pages.body:
The paper needs a way to decide whether some set of directions inside a language model is doing the job a workspace does, rather than merely being readable. Its answer is a list of five functional tests, stated in [[fig-1]] and drawn from the properties that mark [[access-consciousness|conscious access]] in humans: a subset of vector representations counts as workspace-like only if it supports all five.

The order of the five is not arbitrary. Each one closes a gap the previous one leaves open.

### The four positive tests

[[verbal-report]] comes first, because it is the property the [[jacobian-lens|J-lens]] was built to find. Asked what it is thinking about, the model names concepts the workspace holds. Agreement alone would prove little: a readout derived from the model's own output distribution agrees with what the model says by construction, which is the objection [[report-relation-by-construction]] records. So the test is causal. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] that exchanges soccer for rugby just before the answer makes the model report rugby ([[fig-6]]).

Report shows the workspace leading the answer, but the contents were set by the task. [[directed-modulation]] asks whether an instruction alone can set them. Told to hold a concept in mind while copying an unrelated sentence, the model puts that concept at the top of the readout at tokens whose visible text has nothing to do with it, and [[fig-10]] measures the rate against a [[no-instruction-baseline|no-instruction baseline]] near zero. A rival reading is that the instruction re-encodes the stimulus rather than writing to the workspace, and the [[j-orthogonalized-property-probe]] separates the two: the label moves into the workspace while the underlying property probe stays at baseline.

Instructed contents could still be inert decoration. [[internal-reasoning]] tests whether the model computes with them. Exchanging an unspoken intermediate for another one, in lens coordinates only, changes the final answer to the one the substituted concept implies ([[fig-13]]).

That leaves the question of whether one such vector is read by one circuit or by many. [[flexible-generalization]] applies the identical swap across sixteen function templates: four argument categories with four functions each, twelve source-target pairs per template, 192 trials in all. The swap redirects the top answer on 76 of them, and on 101 at double strength. Failures cluster where [[workspace-loading]] was already low before any intervention, which is the paper's own account of its misses rather than a clean result.

### The fifth test is a limit

[[selectivity]] claims the workspace is small and needed for only a fraction of behavior. Testing a limit requires removing the thing, so this property is carried by [[j-space-ablation]], which zeroes the residual stream's projection onto the top J-lens directions across a band of layers. Across the fourteen tasks of [[fig-24]], classification, judging and extraction survive close to normal while tasks resting on silently inferred content collapse. Writing the steps out largely protects arithmetic, which is what [[cot-externalization]] names.

From that split the paper proposes a criterion, [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]]: the workspace is engaged when an intermediate must be handed to an arbitrary, context-specified operation, and not when the computation is automatic. [[fig-20]] is the sharpest case. The same language swap changes the answer under explicit report and flexible computation, but leaves continuation and [[anomaly-detection-condition|anomaly detection]] unchanged, so the representation is present and causally idle at once.

A reader arriving at any member page can now place it: which of the five it serves, and whether it is the demonstration or the control. What the five do not settle is where in the model this happens, which is the subject of the [[layer-bands|layer bands]].

pages.body:
Post-training is the stage that turns a next-token predictor into a chat Assistant. This chapter asks what that stage does to the workspace: what the J-space holds before it, what it holds after, and whether that content can be written on purpose rather than only read.

The starting point is the [[base-model]], trained on next-token prediction alone. Its workspace is already there and already load-bearing. What it does not have is a privileged point of view — the paper calls this [[workspace-self-dissociation]], and takes it to mean that workspace function comes first and a self is a later addition.

### The point of view arrives

[[post-training]] adds the missing piece by training one character's behavior specifically: [[assistant-persona]]. Prior work had found the Assistant represented with the same machinery as any other character, which is the backdrop of [[assistant-as-simulated-character]]. Section 6 qualifies that picture.

The test is a matched comparison: the same prompt, the same lens, a production model and its own pretrained base. On a user's report of taking Tylenol, the post-trained model's readout at a word in the middle of the user's sentence carries safe on a standard dose and unsafe, dangerous, WARNING on an overdose; the base model reads pain, now, feels on both ([[fig-42]]). That is [[assistant-point-of-view]]: an assessment the Assistant would form, present while the model is still reading.

One example is not a result, so the paper fixes a measurement design first — [[reaction-concepts-protocol]]. A short list of reaction words is chosen per prompt suite, the best J-lens rank any of them reaches is recorded, and the user turn is scored separately from the Assistant's own turn. On nine bereavement prompts, sorry and grief rank highly during both models' responses, and highly on the user turn only in the post-trained model ([[fig-43]]). The same split appears for hazard words ([[fig-80]]) and for a deliberately withheld answer ([[fig-81]]).

The reason offered is [[user-token-repurposing-hypothesis]]: a post-trained model is no longer scored on predicting the user's next token, so those positions are free for the Assistant's thoughts.

### Watching its own behavior

If the workspace carries the Assistant's view of the user, it may also carry its view of itself. That is [[assistant-self-monitoring]]. Under [[roleplay-character-drift]], disclaimer and fictional rank highly at the token opening the Assistant's turn, and never in the base model ([[fig-44]]).

The next case uses [[prefill]] to force a commitment the model would not make. In the [[preference-violation-experiment]], BUT rises sharply after the forced choice while the model argues for the prefilled option in 88% of cases and voices no objection ([[fig-45]]).

The [[thought-suppression]] setting pushes furthest. Both models fail to suppress the forbidden concept, but only the post-trained model's workspace also carries damn and failure words — 93% and 82% of trials against 17% and 30% ([[fig-46]]). The paper reads this as [[metacognition]] and says plainly that the reading is more speculative than the others, since the words track the suppression instruction and not demonstrably the failure. Such self-descriptive contents are catalogued as [[metacognitive-representations]].

### Writing the workspace

[[counterfactual-reflection-training]] turns the argument around. If reasoning routes through [[verbalizable-representation]], then changing what the model would say if asked to reflect should change how it reasons when it is not asked.

The corpus is built accordingly ([[reflection-training-corpus]]): ten thousand agentic contexts, each truncated mid-task, each given a [[reflection-question]] and a [[constitution-grounded-reflection]] written from twenty principles sampled out of [[anthropic-constitution]] ([[fig-48]]). Loss falls on the reflection turn only, and at evaluation the question is never asked ([[fig-47]]).

Dishonesty falls from 0.25 to 0.07 on the [[fabrication-honesty-benchmark]] and from 0.38 to 0.05 on the [[deception-benchmark]]. The [[ethics-token-ablation]] tests whether the implanted workspace contents carry the gain: removing 176 lens vectors returns the trained model to 0.22 while leaving the baseline at 0.25 ([[fig-49]]). On the deception benchmark ablation recovers only part of the gain, 0.05 back to 0.23, and the paper reports that causal link as the weaker of the two ([[fig-50]]).

The technique sits against [[deliberative-alignment]], which emits its principles, and closer to [[implicit-chain-of-thought]], whose auxiliary text is dropped at inference; the transfer can also be read as [[out-of-context-reasoning]].

Two benchmarks, one model. The paper states that the breadth of the technique is untested, and that it does not know whether anything more specific than "consider ethical principles here" can be implanted this way. A reader arriving at any member concept from here can place it on one of two questions: what post-training put in the workspace, and what a trainer can put there next.

pages.body:
The paper carries close to a hundred figures, but they are built from about a dozen chart shapes, each reused across many experiments. This chapter explains the shapes rather than the results: what each one plots, why it was drawn that way, and what it would look like if the claim resting on it were false.

Everything starts with the drawing that measures nothing. The [[method-schematic|method and convention schematic]] fixes how the [[jacobian-lens|Jacobian lens]] is built, read and written into, which layers the paper calls the workspace, and how strong each dose of ablation is. [[fig-4]] puts the whole instrument on one page. Later charts inherit its conventions, including depth reported as a percentage of the model's layers rather than a layer count, under [[layer-percentage-indexing|the paper's numbering scheme]].

### Shapes that show what the workspace holds

The [[ranked-readout-panel|ranked lens-readout panel]] is the base case: the top few vocabulary tokens read off one activation, printed as a column. A single column has no scale of its own. That is why the panel almost always appears two or three columns wide, one per condition, and why it reads by which tokens appear and at what rank rather than by the length of any bar.

The [[layer-position-readout-trace|layer-by-layer readout trace]] is that panel run over a whole forward pass, laid out as a grid of token position against layer with the top token printed in each cell. It answers where in the pass a concept appears, not what the model is about to say next.

Printing every readout is not workable for a long transcript. The [[token-shaded-transcript|token-shaded transcript]] collapses each position's readout into a single number and shades the text by it. Each panel's ramp saturates at its own maximum, so the shading ranks positions inside one panel and carries nothing across panels.

That per-panel normalization is exactly why the [[concept-token-detector-plot|concept-token detector plot]] exists. A fixed word list is looked for in the top-k readout at every workspace layer, and the hits are summed into one count per prompt, on a scale that survives comparison across conditions. A control condition sitting flat at zero is what makes the count readable. The [[turn-paired-rank-plot|user-turn versus assistant-turn rank plot]] applies the same aggregation to rank, splitting four bars by whose turn the tokens belong to and by whether the model was post-trained ([[fig-43]]).

Two shapes put depth on the horizontal axis. The [[workspace-band-profile|workspace-band profile]] exists to locate the two depths where a curve changes slope, the edges of [[layer-bands|the sensory, workspace and motor bands]], and a shuffled or random control fixes the zero because the height itself is not the claim ([[fig-31]]). The [[ambiguity-commitment-plot|ambiguity commitment plot]] sweeps a blended input instead, and asks at which layer the trace stops tracking the blend and steps to one end ([[fig-29]]).

### Shapes that test a cause

Readouts are correlational, so the paper pairs them with two intervention shapes. The [[swap-success-chart|swap-success chart]] is a pass/fail scoreboard for the [[lens-coordinate-swap|lens-coordinate swap]]: the fraction of trials on which exchanging two concepts' coordinates moved the swapped-in answer to the model's top-1 output, reported across models, templates and lenses ([[fig-19]]). The [[intervention-vs-control-bars|score-under-intervention bar chart]] prints an intervention beside [[matched-norm-controls|a control perturbation]] matched in size, layer and position ([[fig-86]]). Without that matched bar, an effect could belong merely to how much was removed.

### Shapes that argue from weights and wiring

The [[weights-only-population-comparison|weights-only population comparison]] runs no forward pass at all. Curves for competing populations of directions are plotted against source layer and normalized so a random direction scores 1; the case for [[j-space-broadcast|broadcast privilege]] lives in the gap between populations, not in any curve's height ([[fig-79]]).

The [[three-lens-comparison|three-lens benchmark comparison]] holds its colors fixed — J-lens black, [[logit-lens|logit lens]] red, [[tuned-lens|tuned lens]] blue — and repeats across benchmarks, metrics and swept variables, so no single convenient setting can carry the comparison ([[fig-52]]).

The [[lens-attribution-graph|J-lens attribution graph]] draws one forward pass as nodes and edges, and is paired with swap bars that test whether the drawn wiring is causally real ([[fig-89]]). It shows how a computation is organized, never how large a quantity is.

A reader who has these in hand can open any figure in the paper, name its shape, and state the specific pattern that would have contradicted the claim it is placed under.

Section 3 established what J-space contents can do. This chapter asks what the J-space is as an object in the model: where in depth it does that work, how much it holds, and whether the weights are arranged to spread it.

### Where the band begins and ends

[[j-space|The J-space]] is defined at every layer, so where it acts must be found rather than assumed. The paper compares the J-lens vectors of each pair of layers with [[cka|centered kernel alignment]], which compares their matrices of pairwise similarities. The result falls into three blocks: an early third, a long middle, and a short tail.

Two of those blocks are accounted for in advance. The final layers must encode the next token; the first can encode little beyond the identity of the present one. Anything workspace-like therefore sits in the middle block, which the paper's [[layer-bands|three-band division of depth]] puts at roughly L38 to L92 in Sonnet 4.5 ([[fig-27]]).

[[workspace-boundary-metrics|Four further statistics]], all derived from the lens, place the same two boundaries. An empty early band could therefore mean the lens fails at that depth rather than that the model carries nothing there ([[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]]).

The ambiguity sweep is the check that does not depend on the lens. A concept token's input embedding is replaced by a weighted mixture of two country embeddings. The activation is then scored by its position on the line between that trial's two pure cases. Early layers track the mixture smoothly. From about layer 38 the activation sits near one end or the other and switches sharply between them ([[fig-29]]) — the commitment the paper reads as [[ignition]]. Two prior results locate the same middle region: [[stable-regions|piecewise stability]] under input interpolation, and a [[synergistic-core]] from integrated information decomposition.

### How much it holds

Inside the band, the residual stream is reconstructed as a sparse nonnegative sum of J-lens vectors; the count that still beats a same-size random control is the occupancy. It settles at about 25. The variance those vectors explain in excess of the control never exceeds 10% ([[fig-30]]), so the bulk of the activation lies outside the J-space.

A second measurement asks what the space holds functionally. The model reads 80-word lists while the lens counts which list words are present. Unrelated words hold at roughly six at a time across the band, and at one or two in a [[single-layer-capacity|single layer]], which suggests concepts held at different depths. Related words behave differently. [[category-loading|Nearly the whole word family loads]] within a few items, unread members included. What clears it is [[category-displacement|a new category]], not the passage of tokens ([[fig-31]]).

Those numbers measure the [[workspace-capacity-limit|capacity limit]] [[global-workspace-theory]] posits ([[j-space-capacity]]). The comparison with [[working-memory|human working memory]] holds on one side only. The per-position limit is of a similar order. But attention gives the model lossless access to what it computed earlier, so its workspace never has to sustain state.

### Why the contents travel

A small store matters only if its contents reach the rest of the computation. Across depth, the next [[mlp-block]] amplifies a J-lens direction about ten times more than a random direction, while neuron output directions stay near 1. Across positions, the top 1% of workspace-layer heads both amplify J-lens directions and copy them without scrambling them into one another; those two criteria define the [[broadcast-heads]]. Zeroing those heads cuts recall of the readout's top 25 to 0.67, against 0.86 for random layer-matched sets, and drops the rate of reporting an injected thought from 0.54 to 0.09 ([[fig-34]]). The paper reads [[j-space-broadcast|this]] as [[global-broadcast|broadcast]] built into the weights.

For a sparsity level $k$, the appendix defines the J-space formally: the union over every size-$k$ subset of J-lens vectors of the cone of their nonnegative combinations ([[eq-jspace-cones]]). That [[j-space-formalization|definition]] adds a distance, so two [[workspace-candidate|workspace candidates]] with different vocabularies can be compared by the errors they assign to real activations. Of each claim here, a reader can now ask whether it describes the model or the instrument.
